summary: Defines a limited common set of Diffserv per-hop behaviors and codepoints for connections between separately operated networks, to simplify configuration and operation.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks that carry traffic at different priorities each use their own names and numbers for them, so two networks connecting to each other have to agree what to do with every mark they meet. This document defines four shared classes that can be used at the connection between networks, and a simple way to translate a network's own marks into them and back.

subtitle: A small agreed set of traffic classes and marks that networks can use at the point where they connect to each other.

tldr.problem: Each network picks its own traffic classes and marks, so at a connection between two networks the marks rarely match, and getting the right treatment usually means negotiating and configuring each link separately.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines four interconnection classes, each with the per-hop behaviours and codepoints to use at the interconnect, and maps every class in the service class taxonomy onto one of them.
tldr.outcome: A network maps its internal marks to and from the four agreed marks at every edge, so a packet keeps its treatment from one end of the path to the other, and the mapping only has to be specified once for all interconnections.

today: RFC 8100 is an Informational document published in March 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it requires no IANA actions. It builds on the Diffserv architecture in RFC 2475 and the service class configuration guidelines in RFC 4594.

sections.title: Why Interconnection Needs Its Own Set of Marks
sections.content:
Diffserv has been deployed in many networks. It provides differentiated traffic forwarding based on the Diffserv Codepoint field, which is part of the IP header. This document defines a set of common Diffserv classes, Per-Hop Behaviors, and codepoints for use at interconnection points, to which and from which locally used classes and codepoints should be mapped.

When a packet crosses a domain boundary, the marking may be changed, and this is a Diffserv feature. If traffic marked with unknown or unexpected codepoints is received, the recommendation is to forward it with default, best-effort treatment without changing the markings, to support incremental Diffserv deployment and routers that do not support Diffserv. Many networks do not follow that recommendation and instead re-mark unknown or unexpected codepoints to zero, so that only the right codepoints are used inside a Diffserv domain. This document is based on that latter approach and defines additional codepoints that are known and expected at interconnection interfaces, in order to reduce the amount of traffic whose marks have to be reset.

The document is motivated by requirements for IP interconnection with Diffserv support among providers that operate Multiprotocol Label Switching in their backbones, but it also applies to other technologies. The operational simplifications help align IP Diffserv functionality with the limitations of the widely deployed Short Pipe Model for MPLS tunnel operation. Limiting Diffserv to a small number of Treatment Aggregates can also let traffic leave a network with the codepoint it arrived with, even if a different codepoint is used inside the network, which gives an opportunity to extend consistent Diffserv treatment across network boundaries.

In isolation, using a defined set of interconnection behaviours and codepoints may appear to be extra effort. The offsetting benefit is that the mapping is specified once for all of the interconnections to other networks that can use this approach. Without it, the behaviours and codepoints have to be negotiated and configured independently for each network interconnection, which scales badly. Consistent end-to-end treatment is also more likely to result, because traffic is re-marked to the same codepoints at all interconnections.
sections.plainLanguage: Every network names its own traffic classes in its own way, so the same kind of traffic looks different on each side of a connection. Agreeing a small shared set of classes for the connection itself means each network only has to write down its own translation twice, once for sending and once for receiving, and it gets the same treatment all the way along the path.

sections.title: The Idea: Restore the Mark at Every Interconnection
sections.content:
The interconnection approach, called Diffserv-Intercon, uses a set of Per-Hop Behaviors, mapped to four corresponding MPLS Treatment Aggregates, along with a set of interconnection codepoints that allow straightforward rewriting to domain-internal codepoints and defined codepoint markings for traffic forwarded to interconnected domains.

The basic idea is that traffic sent with a Diffserv-Intercon behaviour and codepoint is restored to that behaviour and codepoint at each network interconnection, even though a different behaviour and codepoint may be used within each network involved. The key requirement is that the network ingress interconnection codepoint be restored at the network egress, and the key observation is that this is only feasible in general for a small number of codepoints. Traffic sent with other codepoints can be re-marked to an interconnection codepoint, or dealt with through an additional agreement between the operators of the interconnected networks.

The document applies to the use of Differentiated Services for interconnection traffic between networks, and is particularly suited to interconnection of MPLS-based networks that use Short Pipe Model tunnels. It also applies to other network technologies, but it is not intended for use within an individual network. It simplifies IP-based interconnection to domains operating the Short Pipe Model, both for traffic terminating inside the domain and for traffic transiting onward to another domain. Transiting traffic is received and sent with the same behaviour and codepoint. Terminating traffic keeps the behaviour it arrived with, although the codepoint may change.

Diffserv-Intercon is also applicable to Pipe Model tunnels, but not to Uniform Model tunnels. The approach defines a set of four behaviours for support at interconnections or network boundaries in general, with corresponding codepoints for use at an interconnection interface. It is extensible by IETF standardization, so additional behaviours and codepoints can be specified later. Coding space for private interconnection agreements or provider internal services is available, because only a single digit number of standard codepoints are applied by the approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network converts its own marks into one of four agreed marks when traffic leaves, and converts them back when traffic arrives. The agreed marks are put back at every edge, so the traffic is treated the same way no matter how many networks it passes through. Only a handful of marks can be handled this way, which is why the set is small.

sections.title: The Four Interconnection Classes
sections.content:
At an interconnection the networks involved need to agree on the behaviours used and the specific codepoint for each. This document defines four interconnection Treatment Aggregates with well-defined codepoints to be aggregated by them. The sending party re-marks codepoints from internal usage to the interconnection codepoints, and the receiving party re-marks codepoints to their internal usage. The interconnection agreement defines the set of codepoints and behaviours supported across the two interconnected domains, and the treatment of behaviours and codepoints that the receiving domain does not recognize.

The Telephony Service Treatment Aggregate carries PHB Expedited Forwarding with codepoint 101 110 and PHB VOICE-ADMIT with codepoint 101 100. It corresponds to the Real-Time Treatment Aggregate in terms of queuing, where both delay and jitter should be minimised, but it is restricted to transport Telephony service class traffic.

The Bulk Real-Time Treatment Aggregate is designed to transport PHB AF41 with codepoint 100 010; the other AF4 behaviours may be used for a future extension of the set of codepoints carried by this aggregate. It is intended to provide interconnection of a subset of the Real-Time Treatment Aggregate, specifically the portions that consume significant bandwidth, expected to consist of the Broadcast Video, Real-Time Interactive and Multimedia Conferencing service classes. It should be configured with a rate-based queue. By comparison with the approach in RFC 5127, the number of codepoints is reduced to one initially, and AF42 and AF43 could be added if there is a need for three-colour marked Multimedia Conferencing traffic.

The Assured Elastic Treatment Aggregate consists of PHBs AF31 and AF32, that is codepoints 011 010 and 011 100; the number of codepoints is reduced to two, with AF33 reserved for extension. The document suggests using it to transport signalling marked by AF31. The Signaling, Multimedia Streaming, Low-Latency Data and High-Throughput Data service classes should be mapped to it.

The Default / Elastic Treatment Aggregate transports the Default behaviour, CS0 with codepoint 000 000. An important difference from RFC 5127 is that any traffic with unrecognized or unsupported codepoints may be re-marked to this codepoint. The Standard and Low-Priority Data service classes should be mapped to it. This document does not specify an interconnection class for Low-Priority Data, so that traffic is re-marked with CS0 at the interconnection, with the effect that it is treated the same as data sent using the Standard class.

Ingress nodes must condition all inbound traffic so that the codepoints are acceptable; packets with unacceptable codepoints must be discarded or have their codepoints modified to acceptable values before being forwarded, for example by resetting the codepoint to CS0 when the traffic comes from a domain with which no enhanced service agreement exists. An interconnection agreement therefore has to specify not only the treatment of traffic that arrives with a supported codepoint but also the treatment of traffic that arrives with unsupported or unexpected codepoints.

While Diffserv-Intercon allows modification of unacceptable codepoints, if traffic using one or more of the behaviours in a PHB group is accepted as part of a supported aggregate, then traffic using other behaviours from the same group should not be modified to use behaviours outside that group, and in particular should not be re-marked to CS0 unless the entire group is re-marked to CS0. This avoids unexpected forwarding behaviour and potential reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: Four classes are defined: telephony, bulk real-time, assured elastic, and everything else. Each names the behaviours and the numbers to use at the connection point, and the document says which kinds of traffic from the wider service taxonomy should go in each. Anything the far end does not recognise is put back to the default class, and a group of related behaviours is never split up.

sections.title: A Worked Example with Three Providers
sections.content:
The example has provider O, provider W and provider F all peered with provider T, with the three of them having agreed a Diffserv interconnection agreement. Traffic from provider O terminates inside provider T's network, while traffic from provider W transits through provider T to provider F. All the providers use their own internal behaviour and codepoint that correspond to the AF31 behaviour in the Diffserv-Intercon Assured Elastic Treatment Aggregate; in the example AF21, CS2 and AF11 are used.

Providers only need to deploy mappings of internal codepoints to and from the Diffserv-Intercon codepoints, so that they can exchange traffic using the desired behaviours. Provider O has decided that the properties of its internal class AF21 are best met by the Assured Elastic Treatment Aggregate, PHB AF31. At the outgoing peering interface with provider T, provider O's peering router re-marks AF21 traffic to AF31. The domain-internal behaviour of provider T that meets the requirement of that aggregate comes from the AF2x group, so AF31 traffic received at the interconnection with provider T is re-marked to AF21 by provider T's peering router, and provider T has chosen to use MPLS TC value 2 for this aggregate. At the penultimate MPLS node, the top MPLS label is removed and exposes the IP header marked with the codepoint set at the network ingress. The peering router connecting provider T with provider F classifies the packet by its provider-T-internal codepoint AF21, and as the packet leaves provider T on the interface to provider F this causes the packet's codepoint to be re-marked to AF31. Provider F's peering router then classifies the packet for its own internal behaviour AF11, which is the behaviour whose properties match the aggregate.

The example extends in two ways. Provider W uses CS2 for traffic that corresponds to the AF31 behaviour, and that traffic is mapped to AF31 at the interconnection with provider T. If provider O also supports a behaviour marked AF22 that is supposed to obtain Diffserv transport within provider T's domain, then provider O re-marks it with AF32 for the interconnection. If provider W supports CS3 for internal use only, no Diffserv-Intercon mapping needs to be configured at the peering router, and traffic sent with CS3 due to a misconfiguration may be re-marked to CS0 by provider T.
sections.plainLanguage: Three networks are connected through a fourth. The first network sends its own internal mark, the shared mark, and its own internal mark again. The middle network does the same for the traffic it passes on, and the third network converts to its own internal mark. Along the way the behaviour is the same, and only the numbers change.

sections.title: Tunnels, Network Control Traffic and Unknown Marks
sections.content:
The document reviews the three tunnel models. With the Uniform Model neither the codepoint nor the behaviour changes, which is outside the scope of this document. With the Pipe Model the inner tunnel codepoint remains unchanged but an outer tunnel codepoint and the behaviour could change, so a packet received with a network-specific CS1 would be transported with the Default behaviour while the CS1 is not rewritten; that model is also outside the scope. With the Short Pipe Model the codepoint likely changes and the behaviour might change, and this is the case the document is written for.

The reason lies in how MPLS Short Pipe tunnels work. PHP removes and discards the provider's label carrying the provider's TC field before traffic exits the provider's network, one hop upstream of the tunnel endpoint, so no provider TC information is available at the tunnel egress. To ensure consistent handling of traffic at the tunnel egress, the codepoint in the encapsulated IP header has to contain one that is valid for the provider's network, so that the IP header cannot carry a different codepoint edge to edge.

Network control traffic is a special case. Within a provider's network the CS6 codepoint is used for local network control traffic, such as routing protocols and Operations, Administration and Maintenance traffic that is essential to network operation. Network control traffic exchanged between networks, such as BGP, usually terminates at or close to a network edge and is not forwarded through the network, and it is unlikely to be covered by standard interconnection agreements, so it is more likely to be configured specifically. The document does not change RFC 4594, but observes that network control traffic received at an ingress is generally different from network control traffic inside a network. Some CS6 traffic exchanged across carrier interconnections is terminated at the ingress node, for example when BGP runs between the two routers at the ends of an interconnection link, and in that case the operators would enter into a bilateral agreement to use CS6 for that BGP traffic. Network control traffic makes sense for a purchased transit agreement, and preserving the CS6 marking for transited network control traffic is reasonable in some cases, although it is generally inappropriate to use CS6 for forwarding that traffic inside the network that provides the transit; an IP tunnel is suggested to conceal the CS6 markings, using the Pipe Model for Diffserv tunnelling.

Interconnecting carriers should specify the treatment of CS6-marked traffic that arrives at an interconnection and is to be forwarded beyond the ingress node. The recommended agreement covers three cases: traffic that is network control traffic for both domains should be classified and marked for CS6; traffic that is network control traffic for the sending domain only should be forwarded with a behaviour appropriate for transiting network control traffic in the receiving domain, such as AF31; and any other CS6-marked traffic should be re-marked or dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of traffic need special handling. Routing traffic between networks, such as BGP, usually stops at the edge, and the two operators have to agree separately to give it the mark that is normally reserved for a network's own control traffic. And when a provider's own label is stripped before the traffic leaves its network, the IP header has to carry a mark that the provider recognises, which is the reason the interconnection codepoints exist at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The codepoint field in the IP header can expose additional traffic classification information at network interconnections, by comparison with using a zero codepoint for all interconnect traffic. If that classification information is sensitive, the codepoint field could be re-marked to zero to hide the classification, at the cost of losing Diffserv information and differentiated traffic handling on the interconnect and subsequent networks. When Assured Forwarding behaviours are used, any such re-marking should respect the PHB group boundaries described earlier.

The document introduces no new features; it describes how to use existing ones, and the Diffserv security considerations in RFC 2475 and RFC 4594 apply. The IANA considerations section says the document requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic mark is itself a piece of information, so a provider that does not want its classification visible at the connection can zero it, at the price of losing the differentiated handling on the rest of the path. The document adds no security rules of its own.

items.title: Unknown codepoints go to CS0
items.text: Traffic with unrecognized or unsupported codepoints may be re-marked to CS0.

items.title: Keep PHB groups together
items.text: Do not move traffic outside its PHB group unless the whole group is re-marked to CS0.

items.title: CS6 for shared control traffic
items.text: Traffic that is network control traffic for both domains should be classified and marked for CS6.

items.title: CS6 for one side only
items.text: Traffic that is control traffic for the sending domain only should be carried with AF31.

items.title: Other CS6 traffic
items.text: Any other CS6-marked traffic should be re-marked or dropped.
